planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Regale is self-fertile and ripens in the mid-season window, pairing well with an earlier variety like Cowart and a later one like Nesbitt for an extended harvest.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Regale is a University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its large, glossy black berries with a thinner skin and juicier, sweeter flesh than many older black muscadine cultivars, making it well suited to fresh eating as well as juice and wine production. Vines are vigorous and productive, ripening a heavy mid-season crop that holds up well on the vine without excessive splitting in wet weather, a common problem with thinner-skinned muscadines. Regale is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, though as with other muscadines, planting several varieties together tends to boost overall yield. It shows good disease resistance typical of muscadine grapes in humid Gulf South conditions, requiring far less fungicide input than bunch grapes. Harvest as berries turn fully black and detach easily from the stem with gentle pressure; expect the vine to reach full production three to four years after planting on a sturdy two-wire trellis.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Georgia

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Delight is self-fertile and ripens early to mid-season, making it a reliable anchor variety for a home muscadine planting.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Delight is a long-established North Carolina State University bronze muscadine cultivar known for consistent production of medium-sized, sweet, thin-skinned bronze berries with good flavor for fresh eating, well ahead of the peak-season bronze varieties like Fry. Vines are vigorous and reliably productive, and the early-to-mid-season ripening window makes Delight useful for extending the start of the bronze muscadine harvest when paired with later cultivars. It is self-fertile and needs no separate pollinizer, though yield improves with additional muscadine varieties nearby. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that limit bunch grape production in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input once established. Harvest as berries color fully and detach easily from the stem; train vines to a sturdy two-wire trellis and prune annually in winter to keep fruiting wood renewed.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Cultivars
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Georgia

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Welder is self-fertile and ripens in the mid-to-late season, and its Gulf Coast Texas origins make it especially well suited to hot, humid growing conditions along the coast.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Welder is a heritage Texas muscadine selection, originally found growing wild along the Texas Gulf Coast, long valued by home growers for its vigorous, reliably productive vines and dark bronze-to-purple berries with the strong, musky-sweet, classic muscadine flavor favored for fresh eating, jelly, and homemade wine. Its Gulf Coast origins give it excellent heat and humidity tolerance, and it has a long track record of thriving with minimal care in Texas and Louisiana home gardens where more refined modern cultivars can sometimes struggle. Welder is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinizer, though yields benefit from having other muscadine vines nearby. Like other muscadines, it shows strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make bunch grapes difficult in the humid South. Harvest as berries darken fully and detach easily from the stem with gentle pressure, and train the vigorous vine to a sturdy two-wire trellis with annual winter pruning.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Muscadine Grapes for Texas
LSU AgCenter Publication — Muscadines for Louisiana Home Gardens
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Georgia

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Granny Val is self-fertile and ripens mid-to-late season, producing very large black berries prized for fresh eating.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Granny Val is a Mississippi State University muscadine release bred for exceptionally large, glossy black berries with a good balance of sweetness and the classic musky muscadine flavor, ranking among the largest-fruited black muscadine cultivars available for home gardens. The large berry size makes it a favorite for fresh eating and an eye-catching addition to a mixed muscadine planting, and vines are vigorous and reliably productive once established on a sturdy trellis. Granny Val is self-fertile and does not need a separate pollinizer, though nearby compatible varieties tend to improve overall yield. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that make bunch grapes difficult to grow in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input. Harvest as berries turn fully black and detach easily from the stem, and prune annually each winter to renew fruiting wood and keep the vigorous vine in bounds.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Production
